concepts.def: A lipid made of a glycerol molecule linked to two fatty acid chains and a phosphate group. The phosphate head is hydrophilic and the two hydrocarbon tails are hydrophobic, so the molecule is amphipathic. Phospholipids are the main lipid of cell membranes.

Describes a molecule that has both a hydrophilic (water-attracting) region and a hydrophobic (water-repelling) region. Phospholipids and other amphipathic lipids naturally arrange themselves in water so that their hydrophilic parts face the water and their hydrophobic parts are kept away from it.

A continuous sheet two molecules thick that phospholipids and other amphipathic lipids form spontaneously in water. The hydrophilic heads of both layers face the aqueous solutions on either side and the hydrophobic tails point inwards, forming a hydrophobic core. The bilayer is held together by hydrophobic interactions and other weak forces, not by covalent bonds between the lipids, and is the basis of all cell membranes.

The central region of a membrane, formed by the hydrocarbon chains of the fatty acids of the two layers of phospholipids. Because it contains no water and no charges, it has low permeability to large molecules and to hydrophilic particles such as ions and polar molecules.

The ease with which a particular substance can cross a membrane. A pure lipid bilayer is readily permeable to small non-polar molecules, only slightly permeable to small polar molecules such as water, and almost impermeable to ions and large polar molecules, so it functions as an effective barrier between the aqueous solutions on its two sides.

The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration as a result of their random movement, without any transport protein and without energy from ATP. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are small non-polar molecules that cross membranes by simple diffusion, passing between the phospholipids of the bilayer.

A membrane protein that is embedded in the lipid bilayer, in one of the two lipid layers or spanning both. The part of the protein within the bilayer has hydrophobic amino acid R-groups on its surface, which interact with the hydrocarbon tails. Integral proteins include channels, pumps, receptors and enzymes.

A membrane protein that is not embedded in the hydrophobic core but is attached to one or other surface of the bilayer, either to the hydrophilic heads of phospholipids or to the exposed part of an integral protein. Peripheral proteins are found on both the cytoplasmic and the extracellular faces of membranes.

The net movement of water molecules across a membrane that is permeable to water but not to the solute, from a solution with a lower solute concentration to a solution with a higher solute concentration. Water molecules move randomly in both directions; the net movement arises because the side with the lower solute concentration has a higher proportion of free water molecules, so more water molecules cross from that side than return.

An integral membrane channel protein with a narrow pore that allows water molecules, but not ions or other solutes, to pass through. Aquaporins greatly increase the permeability of a membrane to water, so cells that must move water rapidly by osmosis, such as some kidney tubule cells, have many aquaporins in their membranes.

The passive movement of particles across a membrane, down their concentration gradient, through a channel protein or carrier protein. It requires no energy from ATP, but because each protein allows only a specific particle through, it makes the membrane selectively permeable to that particle.

An integral protein with a central pore through which specific ions or other hydrophilic particles diffuse across the membrane. The diameter of the pore and the charges on the amino acids lining it determine which particle can pass. Many channels are gated: they can be open or closed, and ions diffuse through only when the channel is open.

The movement of specific particles across a membrane against their concentration gradient, using energy released by the hydrolysis of ATP. It is carried out by pump proteins and stops if the cell can no longer supply ATP.

An integral membrane protein that uses energy from ATP to change its shape and so transfer a specific particle from one side of the membrane to the other. Because energy is supplied, a pump can move its particle from a lower to a higher concentration, which no form of diffusion can do.

The property of a membrane that allows some substances to cross while others cannot. Selectivity comes from the transport proteins: each channel, carrier or pump handles specific particles, so facilitated diffusion and active transport are selective. Permeability by simple diffusion is not selective; it depends only on the size of a particle and on whether it is hydrophobic or hydrophilic.

A membrane protein with a carbohydrate chain covalently attached. The carbohydrate part is always on the extracellular side of the plasma membrane, where it takes part in cell recognition and cell adhesion.

A membrane lipid with a carbohydrate chain covalently attached to its hydrophilic head. Like the carbohydrate of glycoproteins, the carbohydrate of a glycolipid projects from the extracellular surface of the plasma membrane and contributes to cell recognition and cell adhesion.

concepts.term: Cell recognition and cell adhesion (roles of membrane carbohydrates)
concepts.def: The two roles of the carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins and glycolipids. In cell recognition, the pattern of carbohydrates on a cell surface identifies the cell, for example as belonging to the organism's own body. In cell adhesion, carbohydrates and proteins on adjacent cells bind to each other, helping to hold cells together.

The accepted model of membrane structure: a phospholipid bilayer in which phospholipids and proteins can move laterally (fluid), with integral and peripheral proteins scattered irregularly through and on the bilayer (mosaic). A two-dimensional drawing shows the bilayer with hydrophilic heads outwards and hydrophobic tails inwards, integral proteins embedded in it, peripheral proteins on its surfaces, glycoproteins with carbohydrate on the extracellular side and cholesterol between the phospholipids.

concepts.term: Hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions of a membrane
concepts.def: The hydrophilic regions are the two surfaces of the membrane, formed by the phosphate heads of the phospholipids, which face the aqueous cytoplasm on one side and the aqueous extracellular fluid on the other. The hydrophobic region is the core, formed by the hydrocarbon tails of both layers. Membrane proteins likewise have hydrophobic regions where they contact the core and hydrophilic regions where they contact water.

The freedom with which the phospholipids and proteins of a membrane move within the plane of the bilayer. Fluidity depends on temperature and on the composition of the membrane, and must be maintained for membranes to be flexible, to allow vesicles to form and fuse, and for membrane proteins to function.

A fatty acid with one or more double bonds in its hydrocarbon chain, which put a kink in the chain so that neighbouring phospholipids cannot pack closely. Lipids rich in unsaturated fatty acids have lower melting points, so a bilayer containing them stays fluid and therefore flexible at the temperatures a cell experiences, including low temperatures.

A fatty acid with no double bonds in its hydrocarbon chain, so the chain is straight and neighbouring phospholipids pack closely together. Lipids rich in saturated fatty acids have higher melting points, so they make a membrane stronger and less fluid, which is an advantage at higher temperatures. Organisms adjust the ratio of saturated to unsaturated fatty acids in their membranes to suit the temperature of their habitat: for example, fish living in cold water have a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids in their membranes than related fish in warm water.

A steroid lipid found in animal cell membranes, positioned between the phospholipids with its small hydrophilic hydroxyl group next to the phosphate heads and its rigid hydrophobic ring structure and hydrocarbon tail among the fatty acid tails. Cholesterol acts as a modulator (adjustor) of membrane fluidity: at higher temperatures it restricts the movement of phospholipids and so stabilizes the membrane, and at lower temperatures it prevents the fatty acid tails from packing closely and so prevents the membrane from stiffening.

The process in which a region of the plasma membrane surrounds material outside the cell and pinches off to form a vesicle inside the cell. It requires ATP and depends on the fluidity of the membrane. Examples are the engulfing of a bacterium by a phagocytic white blood cell and the uptake of droplets of extracellular fluid.

The process in which a vesicle inside the cell moves to the plasma membrane and fuses with it, releasing the contents of the vesicle outside the cell. It requires ATP and depends on the fluidity of the membrane, which allows the vesicle membrane to merge with the plasma membrane. Examples are the secretion of digestive enzymes by pancreatic cells and the release of neurotransmitter from a neuron at a synapse.

A small sac of fluid enclosed by a single membrane, formed by a region of membrane budding off from a larger membrane. Vesicles can form from and fuse with membranes only because the phospholipid bilayer is fluid and can be reshaped, rejoining as a continuous sheet after pinching off or merging.

A channel protein that opens when a specific neurotransmitter binds to it. The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, in the membrane of a postsynaptic neuron or muscle fibre, opens its pore when two molecules of acetylcholine bind to it, allowing sodium ions to diffuse into the cell down their concentration gradient. The acetylcholine itself does not pass through the channel.

A channel protein that opens or closes in response to a change in the membrane potential rather than to the binding of a chemical. Voltage-gated sodium channels and voltage-gated potassium channels in the membrane of a neuron open when the membrane depolarizes, allowing the ions to diffuse down their concentration gradients; no ATP is used by the channels themselves.

An integral protein that, for each molecule of ATP hydrolysed, moves three sodium ions out of the cell and two potassium ions into the cell, both against their concentration gradients. Binding of sodium ions inside the cell and phosphorylation by ATP change the pump's shape so that the sodium ions are released outside; binding of potassium ions outside and loss of the phosphate return it to its original shape, releasing the potassium ions inside.

A transport protein that moves one type of particle across a membrane in one direction while moving a different type in the opposite direction. The sodium–potassium pump is an exchange transporter that uses ATP to swap sodium ions for potassium ions.

A difference in electrical charge between the two sides of a membrane. In a resting neuron the inside of the membrane is negative relative to the outside. Sodium–potassium pumps are important in generating this potential: they move three positive sodium ions out for every two positive potassium ions in, and they maintain the concentration gradients of the two ions on which the potential depends.

A membrane protein that binds a sodium ion and a glucose molecule on the outside of the cell and transfers both to the inside. The sodium ion moves down its concentration gradient and the energy this releases carries glucose against its concentration gradient. These cotransporters absorb glucose from the lumen of the small intestine into the epithelial cells and reabsorb glucose from the filtrate into the cells lining the nephron.

Movement of a particle against its concentration gradient that is driven not by ATP directly but by the movement of a second particle down a gradient that was itself established by an ATP-using pump. In sodium-dependent glucose cotransport, the sodium gradient is maintained by sodium–potassium pumps, so ATP is used, but only indirectly.

A membrane protein that binds to a cell-adhesion molecule on the surface of an adjacent cell, holding the two cells together so that they can form a tissue. Different forms of CAM are used to build the different types of cell–cell junction.

mcqs.q: Why do phospholipids form a bilayer when they are mixed with water?
options: Hydrophilic heads face the water and hydrophobic tails are shielded from it, so the sheet forms spontaneously.
Enzymes in the cell join the phospholipids together into a sheet, using energy released from ATP.
The whole molecule repels water, so the phospholipids gather away from it as a droplet of oil.
Covalent bonds form between neighbouring phospholipids, linking them into one rigid sheet of molecules.
mcqs.specStatementText: Phospholipids form a bilayer by themselves
mcqs.explain: Phospholipids are amphipathic. In water the most stable arrangement is a continuous sheet two molecules thick with heads towards the water on both sides and tails in the middle, so the bilayer forms naturally with no energy input.
rationales: Phospholipids are amphipathic. In water the most stable arrangement is a continuous sheet two molecules thick with heads towards the water on both sides and tails in the middle, so the bilayer forms naturally with no energy input.
A student who thinks membranes must be built like other cell structures picks this. In fact no enzyme or ATP is needed: amphipathic lipids form bilayers spontaneously in water.

A student who treats a phospholipid as an ordinary fat picks this. In fact the phosphate head is hydrophilic, so the molecules form a sheet with heads in contact with water rather than an oil droplet.
A student who expects a membrane to be a covalent polymer picks this. In fact the phospholipids stay separate molecules held together by weak interactions, which is why the bilayer is fluid.

mcqs.q: A lipid is found to form a continuous sheet-like bilayer when shaken with water. Which property must the lipid have?
options: It must be entirely hydrophobic, so that all of its molecules cluster together away from water.
It must be amphipathic, with a hydrophilic region and a hydrophobic region in each molecule.
It must be able to form covalent bonds with neighbouring lipid molecules in the sheet.
It must be acted on by an enzyme that assembles the molecules into the bilayer.
mcqs.specStatementText: Phospholipids form a bilayer by themselves
mcqs.explain: Only amphipathic lipids form bilayers: the hydrophilic regions face the water on each side and the hydrophobic regions form the core. Phospholipids are the main example in cell membranes.
rationales: A student who thinks lipids are simply water-repelling picks this. In fact an entirely hydrophobic lipid would separate as a droplet; a sheet needs a hydrophilic part that stays in contact with water.
Only amphipathic lipids form bilayers: the hydrophilic regions face the water on each side and the hydrophobic regions form the core. Phospholipids are the main example in cell membranes.
A student who expects the sheet to be a covalent polymer picks this. In fact a bilayer is held together only by hydrophobic interactions and other weak forces.
A student who thinks bilayers must be built picks this. In fact the bilayer forms spontaneously; the test in the stem involves only lipid and water, with no enzyme.

mcqs.q: Which of these particles crosses a pure phospholipid bilayer, with no proteins present, least readily?
options: A carbon dioxide molecule, which is larger than a water molecule
An oxygen molecule, which needs a protein to cross the bilayer
A sodium ion, which is small but charged and hydrophilic
A water molecule, which is very small and also polar
mcqs.explain: The hydrophobic core has very low permeability to hydrophilic particles, including ions and polar molecules. A charged sodium ion cannot enter the hydrocarbon core, so it has the lowest permeability of the four.
rationales: A student who ranks particles by size alone picks this. In fact carbon dioxide is non-polar, so it passes readily between the hydrophobic tails despite its size.
A student who thinks nothing crosses the bilayer without a protein picks this. In fact oxygen is small and non-polar and crosses by simple diffusion between the phospholipids.

The hydrophobic core has very low permeability to hydrophilic particles, including ions and polar molecules. A charged sodium ion cannot enter the hydrocarbon core, so it has the lowest permeability of the four.

A student who thinks water cannot cross a bilayer at all without aquaporins picks this. In fact water is small enough to pass slowly between the phospholipids; a charged ion is far less permeable than water.

mcqs.q: A cell is respiring rapidly, so its internal oxygen concentration is low. How do oxygen molecules enter the cell?
options: They diffuse through a channel protein that is specific for oxygen and opens when needed
They are moved in by a pump protein using ATP, because the cell needs oxygen urgently
They move in and out randomly until the concentrations are equal, then stop moving
They pass between the phospholipids by simple diffusion down their gradient
mcqs.specStatementText: Simple diffusion: no protein, no energy
mcqs.explain: Oxygen and carbon dioxide are the guide's examples of simple diffusion across membranes: the small non-polar molecules pass directly between the phospholipids, with net movement from higher to lower concentration.
rationales: A student who thinks every substance needs a protein picks this. In fact oxygen is small and non-polar and needs no channel; it crosses between the phospholipids.
A student who links proteins and urgency with energy use picks this. In fact oxygen enters by simple diffusion down its concentration gradient, with no protein and no ATP.
A student who thinks diffusion ends when concentrations equalise picks this. In fact molecules keep crossing in both directions; only the net movement becomes zero.

Oxygen and carbon dioxide are the guide's examples of simple diffusion across membranes: the small non-polar molecules pass directly between the phospholipids, with net movement from higher to lower concentration.

mcqs.q: Which statement about membrane proteins is correct?
options: Integral proteins are embedded in one or both lipid layers, while peripheral proteins are attached to a surface.
Integral proteins all span the whole bilayer, while peripheral proteins are embedded in only one layer.
Integral and peripheral proteins are both transport proteins, differing only in the substance they carry.
Glycoproteins carry their carbohydrate on both faces of the membrane, so the two surfaces are identical.
mcqs.explain: This is the distinction the guide makes: integral proteins have part of their structure within the bilayer, in one or both lipid layers; peripheral proteins are attached to one or other surface of the bilayer.
rationales: This is the distinction the guide makes: integral proteins have part of their structure within the bilayer, in one or both lipid layers; peripheral proteins are attached to one or other surface of the bilayer.
A student who equates 'integral' with 'transmembrane' picks this. In fact integral proteins may be embedded in only one layer, and peripheral proteins are not embedded at all.
A student who thinks all membrane proteins transport substances picks this. In fact membrane proteins have diverse functions, including enzymes, receptors and adhesion molecules.
A student who pictures a symmetrical membrane picks this. In fact the carbohydrate of glycoproteins is found only on the extracellular side, so the two faces differ.

mcqs.q: An animal cell with a cytoplasmic solute concentration of 0.30 mol dm⁻³ is placed in a solution with a solute concentration of 0.10 mol dm⁻³. The membrane is impermeable to the solute. What happens?
options: Water leaves the cell by osmosis, because water moves from the higher to the lower solute concentration.
Net water movement is into the cell, because more free water molecules hit the membrane from the outside.
Solute diffuses out of the cell until both sides reach 0.20 mol dm⁻³, and water then follows the solute out.
No water crosses the membrane, because the cell membrane has no aquaporins to let water pass.
mcqs.explain: The solution outside has the lower solute concentration and so a higher proportion of free water molecules. Water molecules move randomly in both directions, but more cross inwards than outwards, so the net movement is into the cell.
rationales: A student who applies 'high to low' to the solute picks this. In fact net water movement is from the lower solute concentration (0.10) to the higher (0.30), so water enters the cell.

The solution outside has the lower solute concentration and so a higher proportion of free water molecules. Water molecules move randomly in both directions, but more cross inwards than outwards, so the net movement is into the cell.
A student who treats osmosis as solute diffusion picks this. In fact the stem says the membrane is impermeable to the solute, so the solute cannot move; it is water that crosses.
A student who thinks aquaporins are the only route for water picks this. In fact water can cross the bilayer slowly without them, so osmosis still occurs; aquaporins only increase its rate.

mcqs.q: Some cells lining the kidney tubules have large numbers of aquaporins in their plasma membranes. What is the effect of these aquaporins?
options: They pump water across the membrane against its gradient, using ATP energy.
They allow water to cross the membrane, which is otherwise impossible for the bilayer.
They greatly increase the rate at which water can cross the membrane by osmosis.
They let water move in the direction the cell needs, whatever the solute concentrations.
mcqs.explain: Aquaporins are channel proteins with a pore that water molecules, but not solutes, can pass through. They make the membrane much more permeable to water, so osmosis is rapid in cells that have many of them.
rationales: A student who assumes any protein-mediated transport uses ATP picks this. In fact aquaporins are channels: water diffuses through them passively.
A student who thinks water cannot cross a bilayer at all picks this. In fact water crosses slowly between phospholipids; aquaporins increase the rate rather than making it possible.

Aquaporins are channel proteins with a pore that water molecules, but not solutes, can pass through. They make the membrane much more permeable to water, so osmosis is rapid in cells that have many of them.
A student who thinks a channel can set the direction of movement picks this. In fact water still moves by osmosis, from lower to higher solute concentration; the aquaporin cannot reverse this.

mcqs.q: A potassium channel in a cell membrane is open. Which statement describes the movement of ions through it?
options: Potassium ions and any other ions of similar size diffuse through the open pore.
Potassium ions are moved through in whichever direction the cell requires.
Potassium ions are carried through using energy from the hydrolysis of ATP.
Potassium ions diffuse through, down their gradient, with no ATP used.
mcqs.explain: A channel provides a hydrophilic route through the hydrophobic core for one specific ion. The ions move by facilitated diffusion, down their concentration gradient, and no energy from ATP is needed.
rationales: A student who sees a channel as a hole picks this. In fact the pore's diameter and the charges lining it allow only potassium ions through, even excluding the smaller sodium ion.
A student who thinks 'facilitated' means the cell can choose the direction picks this. In fact diffusion through a channel is passive and net movement is only down the concentration gradient.
A student who thinks protein-mediated transport always needs ATP picks this. In fact channels are used for facilitated diffusion, which is passive; only pumps use ATP.
A channel provides a hydrophilic route through the hydrophobic core for one specific ion. The ions move by facilitated diffusion, down their concentration gradient, and no energy from ATP is needed.

mcqs.q: Root cells absorb nitrate ions from soil water in which the nitrate concentration is much lower than in the cell. When the roots are deprived of oxygen, nitrate uptake falls sharply. What explains these observations?
options: Nitrate is taken up by pumps using ATP from aerobic respiration, so without oxygen the supply of ATP falls and active transport slows.
Nitrate is taken up by active transport in the same direction as diffusion but faster, and the lack of oxygen slows the diffusion.
Nitrate is taken up by pumps using ATP already present in the cell, so removing oxygen must have affected the channel proteins instead.
Nitrate is taken up by facilitated diffusion through channels, which use ATP to move ions across against the gradient.
mcqs.explain: Uptake against a concentration gradient requires active transport, which uses energy from ATP. ATP is regenerated by cell respiration, so depriving the roots of oxygen reduces ATP supply and the pumps slow down.
rationales: Uptake against a concentration gradient requires active transport, which uses energy from ATP. ATP is regenerated by cell respiration, so depriving the roots of oxygen reduces ATP supply and the pumps slow down.

A student who thinks active transport is just faster diffusion picks this. In fact nitrate is moving from a lower to a higher concentration, which diffusion cannot do in any direction; only pumps using ATP can.

A student who does not connect the ATP used by pumps to respiration picks this. In fact the cell's ATP is regenerated continuously by respiration and is used up within seconds if respiration stops, so removing oxygen from an aerobic cell soon halts active transport.
A student who thinks channels use ATP picks this. In fact facilitated diffusion is passive and cannot move ions against a gradient; that is the role of pumps.

mcqs.q: Artificial vesicles were made from a pure phospholipid bilayer. Oxygen crossed the bilayer rapidly, glucose very slowly and potassium ions hardly at all. When a potassium channel protein was inserted into the bilayer, potassium crossed rapidly but permeability to sodium ions and to glucose did not change. Which conclusion is supported?
options: The pure bilayer was selecting substances that a cell would need, letting oxygen in and keeping out potassium.
The selectivity of the membrane came from the channel protein, while the bilayer discriminated only by size and polarity.
The channel raised permeability to potassium because it is simply a small hole, so sodium ions should have crossed as well.
The bilayer ranked substances by size, which is why the small potassium ion crossed faster than the larger glucose.
mcqs.explain: Permeability by simple diffusion depends only on the size and hydrophilic or hydrophobic properties of particles. Adding a protein raised permeability to one specific ion and nothing else, which is selective permeability by facilitated diffusion.
rationales: A student who thinks the membrane makes choices picks this. In fact the bilayer has no way to know what a cell needs; oxygen crossed because it is small and non-polar, potassium did not because it is an ion.

Permeability by simple diffusion depends only on the size and hydrophilic or hydrophobic properties of particles. Adding a protein raised permeability to one specific ion and nothing else, which is selective permeability by facilitated diffusion.
A student who sees the channel as an unselective hole picks this, but the data show sodium permeability unchanged. In fact the channel's structure admits only potassium ions.

A student who thinks size is the only factor picks this, but the data show potassium crossing more slowly than glucose, not faster. In fact the charge on the ion makes it the least permeable of the three.

mcqs.q: Which statement about glycoproteins in the plasma membrane is correct?
options: Their carbohydrate is on the cytoplasmic side and is respired when the cell lacks glucose.
Their carbohydrate projects from both faces of the membrane so that either face can be recognised.
Their carbohydrate is on the extracellular side and is used in cell recognition and adhesion.
They are transport proteins whose carbohydrate forms the channel through which sugars enter the cell.
mcqs.explain: Glycoproteins are proteins with a carbohydrate chain attached. The carbohydrate is located on the extracellular side of the membrane, where its roles are cell recognition and cell adhesion.
rationales: A student who treats every carbohydrate as an energy store picks this. In fact membrane carbohydrates face outwards and serve in recognition and adhesion; they are not respired.
A student who pictures a symmetrical membrane picks this. In fact the carbohydrate is only on the extracellular face; the cytoplasmic face carries no carbohydrate.
Glycoproteins are proteins with a carbohydrate chain attached. The carbohydrate is located on the extracellular side of the membrane, where its roles are cell recognition and cell adhesion.

A student who assumes every membrane protein is a transporter, and reads 'glyco' as meaning it carries sugar, picks this. In fact the carbohydrate of a glycoprotein is a short chain attached to the outer face of the protein for recognition and adhesion; it forms no channel, and sugars cross through separate transport proteins.

mcqs.q: A student draws a two-dimensional representation of the fluid mosaic model. Which feature of the drawing is correct?
options: The tails of the inner layer point into the cytoplasm, as the cytoplasm is the inside of the cell.
The proteins are drawn at regular, equal spacings, like tiles set in a fixed pattern across the sheet.
Glycoproteins are drawn with their carbohydrate chains on the cytoplasmic side of the membrane.
Cholesterol is drawn among the phospholipids within the bilayer, not on its surface.
mcqs.explain: Cholesterol is one of the components the drawing must include, and it is positioned within the bilayer among the phospholipids. The hydrophilic heads form both surfaces and the hydrophobic tails form the core.
rationales: A student who confuses the interior of the bilayer with the interior of the cell picks this. In fact the cytoplasm is aqueous, so the inner layer's heads face it and both sets of tails meet in the middle.
A student who takes 'mosaic' to mean a fixed tiled pattern picks this. In fact the proteins are scattered irregularly and can move laterally.
A student who has not learnt that the two faces differ picks this. In fact the carbohydrate of a glycoprotein is drawn on the extracellular side only.

Cholesterol is one of the components the drawing must include, and it is positioned within the bilayer among the phospholipids. The hydrophilic heads form both surfaces and the hydrophobic tails form the core.

mcqs.q: Membrane proteins from a mouse cell and from a human cell were labelled with different coloured markers and the two cells were fused. After about 40 minutes the two colours were fully intermixed over the surface of the fused cell. What does this show?
options: Proteins can move laterally through the bilayer, so the membrane is fluid and proteins are not held in a fixed pattern.
The membrane developed gaps as it became more fluid, allowing the labelled proteins to leak through them.
The proteins from the two cells were covalently bonded into a single new continuous sheet during fusion.
The proteins remained in fixed positions but the mosaic pattern was rearranged by the fusion event.
mcqs.explain: If the proteins had been fixed in place, each colour would have stayed on its own half. Their mixing shows that proteins move sideways through the fluid phospholipid bilayer, which is what 'fluid' means in the fluid mosaic model.
rationales: If the proteins had been fixed in place, each colour would have stayed on its own half. Their mixing shows that proteins move sideways through the fluid phospholipid bilayer, which is what 'fluid' means in the fluid mosaic model.
A student who thinks 'fluid' means leaky picks this. In fact the bilayer stays continuous; proteins mixed by moving sideways within the plane of the membrane, not through gaps in it.
A student who expects membrane components to be covalently linked picks this. In fact no bonds form between the proteins; they mix because the bilayer is fluid and they can diffuse through it.
A student who thinks 'mosaic' means a fixed arrangement picks this. In fact the proteins moved: fusion joins the membranes but does not move a protein from one half to the other.

mcqs.q: Why does a lipid bilayer that contains a high proportion of unsaturated fatty acids remain fluid at low temperatures?
options: The double bonds hold neighbouring tails rigidly together, giving the bilayer a fixed structure.
The kinked tails cannot pack closely, so the lipids have a lower melting point.
The bilayer's fluidity does not depend on temperature, so its fatty acids make no difference.
The unsaturated tails are straighter than saturated tails, so they slide past one another easily.
mcqs.explain: Each double bond puts a kink in the hydrocarbon chain, so neighbouring phospholipids cannot pack tightly. Lipids with unsaturated fatty acids therefore have lower melting points, and the membrane stays fluid and flexible at temperatures that would solidify a saturated bilayer.
rationales: A student who reasons that a double bond makes the tails stiffer and more rigid picks this. In fact the double bond kinks the tail so the tails pack less closely, which lowers the melting point.

Each double bond puts a kink in the hydrocarbon chain, so neighbouring phospholipids cannot pack tightly. Lipids with unsaturated fatty acids therefore have lower melting points, and the membrane stays fluid and flexible at temperatures that would solidify a saturated bilayer.
A student who thinks fluidity is fixed picks this. In fact a bilayer stiffens as temperature falls, and the fatty acid composition determines the temperature at which this happens.

A student who has the two structures the wrong way round picks this. In fact saturated tails are the straight ones and pack closely; the double bonds of unsaturated tails kink them, and it is the kinks, not straightness, that keep the tails apart.

mcqs.q: In an investigation, fish of one species were kept at 5 °C or at 25 °C for several weeks. The membrane phospholipids of the fish kept at 5 °C contained a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids than those of the fish kept at 25 °C. What is the best explanation?
options: At 5 °C unsaturated fatty acids are needed to make the membranes more rigid, so that they hold their shape firmly in the cold.
At 5 °C the extra unsaturated fatty acids insulate the cells against heat loss, as fat does in polar animals.
At 5 °C membranes rich in saturated fatty acids would stiffen, so the fish increase unsaturated ones to stay fluid.
At 5 °C the fish's membranes are already more fluid because of the cold, so unsaturated fatty acids are added to make them stronger.
mcqs.explain: Unsaturated fatty acids have lower melting points, so a higher proportion keeps the membrane fluid and flexible at the low temperature. Organisms living in cold habitats show the same pattern as an adaptation: cold-water fish have a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids in their membranes than related warm-water fish.
rationales: A student who has swapped the effects of the two types of fatty acid picks this. In fact unsaturated fatty acids lower the melting point and make membranes more fluid, not more rigid.
A student who thinks in terms of insulating fat picks this. In fact a membrane two molecules thick provides no insulation; the change in composition is about keeping the bilayer fluid.

Unsaturated fatty acids have lower melting points, so a higher proportion keeps the membrane fluid and flexible at the low temperature. Organisms living in cold habitats show the same pattern as an adaptation: cold-water fish have a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids in their membranes than related warm-water fish.
A student who reverses the effect of temperature on fluidity picks this. In fact cold makes a bilayer less fluid, not more, and it is saturated fatty acids that add strength.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes cholesterol in an animal cell membrane?
options: It lies within the bilayer between phospholipids and acts solely to reduce membrane fluidity.
It is attached to the outer surface of the bilayer and makes the membrane stiffer and stronger.
It is attached to the outer surface of the bilayer and carries carbohydrate used in cell recognition.
It lies in the bilayer between phospholipids and adjusts fluidity in both directions.
mcqs.explain: Cholesterol is positioned between the phospholipids, hydroxyl group towards the heads and rings among the tails. It is a modulator of fluidity: it stabilizes the membrane at higher temperatures and prevents stiffening at lower temperatures.
rationales: A student who knows cholesterol reduces fluidity at high temperatures but not the rest picks this. In fact at low temperatures it prevents the tails from packing and so stops the membrane stiffening.

A student who pictures cholesterol as an extra on the surface picks this. In fact it is a mostly hydrophobic lipid embedded among the fatty acid tails, and its effect on fluidity depends on temperature.
A student who places cholesterol outside the bilayer and confuses it with a glycolipid picks this. In fact cholesterol carries no carbohydrate and sits within the bilayer.

Cholesterol is positioned between the phospholipids, hydroxyl group towards the heads and rings among the tails. It is a modulator of fluidity: it stabilizes the membrane at higher temperatures and prevents stiffening at lower temperatures.

mcqs.q: Two artificial membranes are made from the same phospholipids, one with cholesterol added and one without. Both are cooled to a temperature at which the membrane without cholesterol becomes stiff. What is expected for the membrane with cholesterol?
options: It remains more fluid than the membrane without cholesterol, because cholesterol prevents the tails from packing closely.
It becomes stiffer than the membrane without cholesterol, because cholesterol reduces fluidity at any temperature.
It is unchanged, because cholesterol on the membrane surface cannot affect the packing of the tails inside.
It is unchanged, because a membrane's fluidity depends only on its fatty acids and not on temperature.
mcqs.explain: At lower temperatures cholesterol, sitting between the phospholipids, keeps the fatty acid tails from packing together, so it prevents the membrane from stiffening. This is the low-temperature half of its role as a modulator of fluidity.
rationales: At lower temperatures cholesterol, sitting between the phospholipids, keeps the fatty acid tails from packing together, so it prevents the membrane from stiffening. This is the low-temperature half of its role as a modulator of fluidity.
A student who thinks cholesterol always reduces fluidity picks this. In fact its effect depends on temperature: it prevents stiffening in the cold and reduces fluidity only at higher temperatures.
A student who places cholesterol on the surface picks this. In fact cholesterol lies among the tails, which is exactly why it can change how closely they pack.
A student who thinks fluidity is fixed picks this, but the stem itself says cooling stiffened the cholesterol-free membrane. In fact temperature, fatty acids and cholesterol all affect fluidity.

mcqs.q: A phagocytic white blood cell engulfs a bacterium, enclosing it in a vesicle inside the cell. Which statement about this process is correct?
options: It is endocytosis, in which the membrane is deformed and pinched off without needing any ATP.
It is endocytosis, which depends on the membrane being fluid enough to bend, pinch off and re-seal.
It is endocytosis, in which the bacterium is pulled in through a large channel protein into a vesicle.
It is exocytosis, in which a section of rigid membrane breaks away cleanly around the bacterium.
mcqs.specStatementText: Vesicles form and fuse because membranes are fluid (HL)
mcqs.explain: Engulfing a bacterium is an example of endocytosis. The phospholipid bilayer must be fluid so that it can surround the bacterium, pinch off as a vesicle and re-form a continuous plasma membrane; the process uses ATP.
rationales: A student who thinks only pump-based transport is active picks this. In fact endocytosis requires ATP to reshape the membrane and move the vesicle.

Engulfing a bacterium is an example of endocytosis. The phospholipid bilayer must be fluid so that it can surround the bacterium, pinch off as a vesicle and re-form a continuous plasma membrane; the process uses ATP.
A student who fits all transport into the channel picture picks this. In fact nothing passes through the bilayer: the membrane wraps around the bacterium and forms the vesicle.

A student who sees vesicle formation as a rigid piece snapping off picks this, and has also reversed the terms. In fact material entering the cell is endocytosis, and it needs a fluid, not a rigid, membrane.

mcqs.q: At a synapse, neurotransmitter stored in vesicles is released into the synaptic cleft. How does the neurotransmitter leave the presynaptic neuron?
options: The vesicle bursts inside the neuron and the neurotransmitter diffuses out through the lipid bilayer.
The vesicle docks at a channel protein through which the neurotransmitter is passed out of the cell.
The vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane by exocytosis, releasing the contents outside.
The vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane, a passive process since no pump protein is involved.
mcqs.specStatementText: Vesicles form and fuse because membranes are fluid (HL)
mcqs.explain: Neurotransmitter release is an example of exocytosis: the vesicle moves to the plasma membrane, the two fluid bilayers merge and the neurotransmitter is released into the synaptic cleft. The process requires ATP.
rationales: A student who pictures 'release' as bursting picks this. In fact the vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and its contents are released outside without crossing a bilayer.
A student who expects all export to go through a protein picks this. In fact exocytosis involves fusion of two fluid membranes, not passage through a channel.

Neurotransmitter release is an example of exocytosis: the vesicle moves to the plasma membrane, the two fluid bilayers merge and the neurotransmitter is released into the synaptic cleft. The process requires ATP.
A student who thinks 'no pump' means 'passive' picks this. In fact exocytosis requires ATP to move the vesicle and bring about fusion, so it is an active process.

mcqs.q: Acetylcholine released at a synapse binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. What happens as a result?
options: The receptor opens and the acetylcholine molecules pass through it into the postsynaptic neuron.
The receptor uses ATP to pump sodium ions into the postsynaptic neuron, depolarizing it.
The receptor stays closed until the membrane potential changes, then it opens.
The receptor's channel opens and sodium ions diffuse into the neuron down their gradient.
mcqs.explain: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is a neurotransmitter-gated ion channel. Binding of acetylcholine changes its shape and opens a pore, and sodium ions diffuse into the cell down their concentration gradient, depolarizing the membrane.
rationales: A student who thinks the neurotransmitter travels through the channel picks this. In fact acetylcholine stays bound on the outside; it is sodium ions that pass through the open pore.
A student who thinks ion movement in neurons is powered by ATP picks this. In fact the receptor is a channel, not a pump: sodium ions diffuse in down their gradient.

A student who has merged the two kinds of gated channel picks this. In fact the nicotinic receptor is opened by acetylcholine binding; it is the voltage-gated channels that respond to the change in potential.

The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is a neurotransmitter-gated ion channel. Binding of acetylcholine changes its shape and opens a pore, and sodium ions diffuse into the cell down their concentration gradient, depolarizing the membrane.

mcqs.q: Which statement about voltage-gated sodium channels in the membrane of a neuron is correct?
options: They open in response to a change in membrane potential and allow sodium ions to diffuse down their gradient.
They open when acetylcholine binds to them and allow sodium ions to diffuse down their gradient.
They open in response to a change in membrane potential and pump sodium ions in using ATP.
They open whenever any small ion is present and allow it to pass through into the neuron.
mcqs.explain: A voltage-gated channel responds to depolarization of the membrane, not to a chemical signal. When open it allows facilitated diffusion of sodium ions down their concentration gradient, using no ATP.
rationales: A voltage-gated channel responds to depolarization of the membrane, not to a chemical signal. When open it allows facilitated diffusion of sodium ions down their concentration gradient, using no ATP.
A student who has merged the two types of gated channel picks this. In fact acetylcholine opens the nicotinic receptor; voltage-gated channels respond only to the membrane potential.
A student who thinks these channels need energy picks this. In fact they are channels for passive diffusion; ATP is used by the sodium–potassium pump, not by the channel.
A student who sees channels as unselective holes picks this. In fact the channel is specific for sodium ions and opens only in response to a change in membrane potential.

mcqs.q: Which sequence correctly describes one cycle of the sodium–potassium pump?
options: Three potassium ions bind inside; ATP phosphorylates the pump; they are released outside; two sodium ions then bind and are released inside.
Three sodium ions bind inside; ATP phosphorylates the pump; they are released outside; two potassium ions bind and are released inside.
One sodium ion binds inside; ATP phosphorylates the pump; it is released outside; one potassium ion binds and is released inside.
Three sodium ions bind inside; the pump opens when the membrane potential changes; they diffuse out; two potassium ions diffuse in.
mcqs.explain: Sodium ions bind on the cytoplasmic side, ATP phosphorylates the pump and changes its shape so the sodium is released outside; potassium ions then bind, the phosphate is lost and the pump returns to its original shape, releasing potassium inside. The exchange is 3 sodium out for 2 potassium in.
rationales: A student who has the directions reversed picks this. In fact it is sodium ions that bind inside and are released outside, and potassium ions that bind outside and are released inside.

Sodium ions bind on the cytoplasmic side, ATP phosphorylates the pump and changes its shape so the sodium is released outside; potassium ions then bind, the phosphate is lost and the pump returns to its original shape, releasing potassium inside. The exchange is 3 sodium out for 2 potassium in.
A student who takes 'exchange' to mean a one-for-one swap picks this. In fact the ratio is three sodium ions out to two potassium ions in, which is why the pump moves net charge.
A student who confuses the pump with a voltage-gated channel picks this. In fact the pump is driven by ATP hydrolysis, not by a change in potential, and it moves both ions against their gradients.

mcqs.q: Epithelial cells from the small intestine were treated with a substance that inhibits sodium–potassium pumps. Uptake of glucose from the lumen by the cells fell sharply, although the sodium-dependent glucose cotransporters themselves were not affected by the substance. What explains this result?
options: The inhibitor stopped the cotransporters hydrolysing ATP, which they need to move glucose against its gradient.
Glucose is normally absorbed by simple diffusion, and the inhibitor made the lipid bilayer impermeable to it.
Without the pumps, sodium accumulated in the cells, so there was no sodium gradient to drive glucose uptake.
The pumps normally carry glucose into the cell, so inhibiting them removed the main route for glucose.
mcqs.explain: The cotransporter moves glucose against its gradient only because sodium ions flow in down theirs. Sodium–potassium pumps maintain that gradient by using ATP to remove sodium from the cell, so inhibiting the pumps removes the gradient and glucose uptake fails. This is why the transport is called indirect active transport.
rationales: A student who thinks the cotransporter uses ATP directly picks this, but the stem says the cotransporters were unaffected. In fact they never hydrolyse ATP; they use the sodium gradient.
A student who thinks glucose diffuses through the bilayer picks this. In fact glucose is polar and cannot cross the bilayer; it needs the cotransporter, and the bilayer was not changed.

The cotransporter moves glucose against its gradient only because sodium ions flow in down theirs. Sodium–potassium pumps maintain that gradient by using ATP to remove sodium from the cell, so inhibiting the pumps removes the gradient and glucose uptake fails. This is why the transport is called indirect active transport.
A student who has not learnt what the pump carries picks this. In fact the pump moves only sodium and potassium ions; glucose enters through the cotransporter, which depends on the pump indirectly.

mcqs.q: How do cells lining the nephron reabsorb glucose from the filtrate when the glucose concentration inside the cells is already higher than in the filtrate?
options: Glucose diffuses in through the lipid bilayer down its own concentration gradient
A cotransporter hydrolyses ATP directly to move glucose in against its gradient
Sodium–potassium pumps carry glucose into the cell together with the potassium
A cotransporter moves glucose in with sodium ions moving down their gradient
mcqs.explain: Sodium-dependent glucose cotransporters bind a sodium ion and a glucose molecule together. Sodium moving down its concentration gradient, maintained by sodium–potassium pumps, provides the energy to move glucose into the cell against its gradient. This is indirect active transport.
rationales: A student who thinks glucose crosses membranes by simple diffusion picks this. In fact glucose is polar, and here it is moving from a lower to a higher concentration, which diffusion cannot do.
A student who applies 'against the gradient means ATP' to the cotransporter itself picks this. In fact the cotransporter uses the sodium gradient; ATP is used only by the sodium–potassium pump.
A student who is unsure what the pump transports picks this. In fact the pump moves only sodium and potassium ions; glucose is carried by a separate cotransporter.

Sodium-dependent glucose cotransporters bind a sodium ion and a glucose molecule together. Sodium moving down its concentration gradient, maintained by sodium–potassium pumps, provides the energy to move glucose into the cell against its gradient. This is indirect active transport.

mcqs.q: How do adjacent cells adhere to one another to form a tissue?
options: Cell-adhesion molecules in each cell's membrane bind to those on the neighbouring cell, with different CAMs used for different junctions.
The fluid plasma membranes of the two cells fuse where they touch, so the two cells share one continuous membrane.
A single universal cell-adhesion molecule links every cell to its neighbours in every type of tissue in the body.
The carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins on one cell are covalently bonded to the lipid bilayer of the adjacent cell.
mcqs.explain: Adhesion is due to CAMs, membrane proteins that bind to matching CAMs on the adjacent cell to form cell–cell junctions. Different forms of CAM are used for different types of junction, giving tissues junctions with different properties.
rationales: Adhesion is due to CAMs, membrane proteins that bind to matching CAMs on the adjacent cell to form cell–cell junctions. Different forms of CAM are used for different types of junction, giving tissues junctions with different properties.
A student who extends membrane fusion from vesicles to whole cells picks this. In fact the membranes of adjacent cells remain separate and are linked by proteins.
A student who takes 'CAM' to be one molecule picks this. In fact there are different forms of CAM, and different forms are used for the different types of cell–cell junction.
A student who reaches for covalent bonds to explain any strong attachment picks this. In fact adhesion depends on non-covalent binding between CAM proteins on the two cells.

mcqs.q: A neuron is treated with a drug that inhibits sodium–potassium pumps. Over the following hours its resting membrane potential declines steadily towards zero. Why does inhibiting the pump have this effect?
options: The drug must also be blocking ion channels, because the pump exchanges one sodium ion for one potassium ion and so cannot affect the potential.
The pump normally exports three sodium ions for every two potassium ions imported, so its net export of positive charge and the ion gradients it maintains are lost.
The pump normally moves sodium ions in and potassium ions out, so without it sodium ions no longer enter and the inside of the cell loses positive charge.
The pump normally opens in response to a change in membrane potential, so without it the voltage-gated channels cannot restore the resting state after an impulse.
mcqs.explain: Sodium–potassium pumps are important in generating membrane potentials: each cycle moves three positive ions out and two in, and the sodium and potassium gradients this builds are what the resting potential depends on. Without the pump the gradients run down and the potential decays.
rationales: A student who takes 'exchange' to mean a one-for-one swap picks this. In fact the exchange is 3:2, so the pump moves net positive charge out of the cell, and the gradients it maintains are what the potential depends on.

Sodium–potassium pumps are important in generating membrane potentials: each cycle moves three positive ions out and two in, and the sodium and potassium gradients this builds are what the resting potential depends on. Without the pump the gradients run down and the potential decays.
A student who has the directions reversed picks this. In fact the pump moves sodium out and potassium in; without it sodium leaks in and potassium leaks out, and the potential collapses.

A student who confuses the pump with a voltage-gated channel picks this. In fact the pump is driven by ATP hydrolysis, not by a change in potential, and it maintains the gradients that the channels rely on.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic B2.1 Membranes and membrane transport

specStatements.text: Phospholipids form a bilayer by themselves
Simple diffusion: no protein, no energy
Vesicles form and fuse because membranes are fluid (HL)

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Glycoproteins and glycolipids are treated only as a carbohydrate chain covalently linked to a membrane protein or lipid, positioned on the extracellular face, with roles in cell adhesion and cell recognition. No named glycoproteins, blood-group antigens, specific oligosaccharide structures, the glycocalyx as a term, or mechanisms of carbohydrate attachment in the Golgi apparatus are included.

Cell adhesion is tested only through the general idea that cell-adhesion molecules (CAMs) in the membranes of adjacent cells bind to each other and that different forms of CAM are used for different types of cell–cell junction. No CAM family (such as cadherins or integrins) and no junction type (such as tight, gap or anchoring junctions) is named or described anywhere in the bank.
